content.title: About
content.content: Chard is a leafy vegetable from the Amaranthaceae family, widely used in Eastern European and Asian cuisines. When cooked, it becomes tender and has a mildly sour flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chard contains oxalates, which in excess may contribute to kidney stone formation.
In Russia, chard is often added to soups such as shchi and cold appetizers.
Its vitamin C content is higher than that of most leafy greens.
Chard can serve as a natural green coloring agent due to its chlorophyll.
The earliest references to chard appear in ancient Greek medical texts.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and participates in collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron is necessary for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Chard is low in calories, making it a good choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids in chard help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High oxalate content
items.content: People prone to kidney stones should limit their intake of chard.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergy to chard.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Oxalates can reduce the absorption of certain minerals such as calcium and magnesium.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chard is typically boiled for 5–10 minutes until tender, then added to soups, stews, omelets, or served as a side dish. It can also be made into a creamy chard dip by blending cooked chard with cottage cheese and sour cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh chard in the refrigerator in a perforated bag with a slight moisture to keep it fresh for 3–5 days. Cooked chard should be placed in an airtight container and kept in the fridge for up to 2 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken thigh prepared by rotisserie cooking with the skin left on is a juicy piece of meat with a crispy crust. The skin retains some fat, making the dish more flavorful and nutrient‑dense. It is often sold as a ready‑to‑eat product in supermarkets and restaurants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rotisserie cooking allows the meat to cook evenly while staying moist.
Chicken skin contains beneficial fatty acids but also adds extra calories.
Thighs are rich in protein and iron, making them a valuable nutrient source.
Traditionally the meat is cooked on a spit over an open flame, giving it a smoky aroma.
In some cultures chicken thighs with skin are considered a delicacy served on special occasions.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken thigh provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Iron from the meat helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels and energy.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nervous system function and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Provides zinc
items.content: Zinc contributes to immune health and wound healing.

items.title: Skin supplies healthy fats
items.content: The skin contains monounsaturated fats that can be part of a balanced diet.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The skin adds significant calories and fat, so portion control is important.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Excess saturated fat intake may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Food‑borne bacteria risk
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking can lead to salmonella or campylobacter contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken thigh with skin can be eaten hot, sliced into pieces, added to salads, sandwiches, or used in tacos. The skin can be eaten if crispy, or removed according to preference.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked product in the refrigerator at 4 °C or below, in an airtight container, for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage freeze in a bag at –18 °C, where it remains good for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Guacamole is a traditional Mexican dip made from ripe avocado, lime juice, salt, onion, tomato, and spices. The NFS (Not From Store) version is a ready‑to‑eat mix packaged in a convenient pouch.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Avocado, the main ingredient, is often called "alligator pear" because of its buttery texture and high monounsaturated fat content.
Traditional guacamole is mashed by hand using a wooden molcajete.
In Mexico, guacamole is commonly served with corn tortilla chips or used as a topping for tacos.
There are over 500 avocado varieties, but the Hass type is preferred for guacamole due to its creamy flesh.
The healthy fats in guacamole help increase the absorption of fat‑soluble nutrients from other foods.

items.title: Rich in healthy fats
items.content: Avocado provides monounsaturated fatty acids that support heart health and help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in blood‑pressure regulation and muscle function.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber promotes digestive health and contributes to satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Guacamole supplies vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Avocado allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to avocado, ranging from skin rash to swelling.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Because of its fat content, guacamole is relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advised for weight‑managed diets.

items.title: Oxidation
items.content: Once opened, guacamole can brown due to oxidation; keep it refrigerated and consume within a few days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Guacamole can be enjoyed as a dip with chips, spread on sandwiches, burgers, salads, or used as a sauce for Mexican dishes. Garnish with fresh cilantro, lime wedges, or diced tomato for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store guacamole in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in its original pouch or an airtight container. Adding a splash of lime juice helps slow browning. Once opened, it remains good for 3‑5 days.
